e.etymology: A respelling of Blakely, an English surname and place name from Old English blaec, 'black, dark', plus leah, 'woodland clearing'.
A recent American blend of Nova with the -lynn ending. Nova is Latin for 'new' and the astronomers' word for a star that suddenly flares bright.

From an English surname, originally Randson, 'son of Rand', a short form of Randolph. It matched the word ransom, with its echo of Christian redemption, and was a fairly common American first name in the 1800s.
namesakes: Ransom Drysdale (Chris Evans's character in Knives Out)

assoc.t: ransom, the payment demanded for a hostage

e.note: It is the everyday word for a kidnapper's payment demand, which most people will hear first.

e.etymology: A spelling of Laken, a name built on the word lake that American parents took up from Laken Lockridge, a character on the 1980s soap opera Santa Barbara.
A Spanish elaboration of Gracia, 'grace', from Latin gratia, with the diminutive ending -ela. The Italian counterpart is Graziella.
A modern American name that joins Kay, or the Kai- of Kaitlyn and Kayla, to Lynn. It is one of many spellings alongside Kaylin, Kailyn and Kaelyn.
The English word, from Old English blostm, 'flower'. It began as an endearment for a little girl and joined the flower names the Victorians made fashionable.
namesakes: Blossom Russo (title character of the 1990s sitcom Blossom)

assoc.t: Blossom, leader of the Powerpuff Girls
Blossom, 1990s NBC sitcom starring Mayim Bialik

e.etymology: From Arabic na'im, 'ease, comfort, bliss', a word also used for the delights of paradise. Hebrew has the related word na'im, 'pleasant'.
From Arabic halima, the feminine of halim, 'gentle, patient, slow to anger'. Halima al-Sa'diyya was the foster mother who nursed the Prophet Muhammad.
A modern American name in the pattern of Kamari, Kalani and Imani. Kamani is also the Hawaiian name of a large coastal shade tree.
From Arabic lin, 'softness, tenderness, gentleness'. In the Netherlands Leen is an unrelated short form of Heleen for girls and Leendert for boys.

A spelling of Harlow, an English place name and surname from Old English here, 'army', or haer, 'rock', plus hlaew, 'hill'. The -e form is the surname of the heroine of Samuel Richardson's novel Clarissa.
A modern elaboration of Eliana or Elian with a new ending, used in Spanish-speaking families. It has no separate meaning of its own.
A transliteration of the Persian and Arabic name Yasmin, from Persian yasamin, the jasmine flower. English Jasmine comes from the same word.
A phonetic respelling of Isaiah, from Hebrew Yesha'yahu, 'the Lord is salvation', the name of the Old Testament prophet.
The Serbian and Macedonian form of John, from Greek Ioannes and Hebrew Yochanan, 'God is gracious'. American parents took it up in the 1970s, usually saying it joh-VAHN.

assoc.t: Jovan, drugstore fragrance line known for Jovan Musk

e.etymology: A modern elaboration of Audrey with the -ina ending of Sabrina and Adriana. V. C. Andrews used it in her 1982 novel My Sweet Audrina, and reality star Audrina Patridge of The Hills carried it to its 2011 peak.
namesakes: Audrina Patridge (reality TV star of The Hills)

e.etymology: A respelling of Clara influenced by Claire. Clara is Latin clara, 'bright, clear, famous', made popular by the 13th-century Saint Clare of Assisi.
A spelling of Ailen, a name from Mapudungun, the Mapuche language of Chile and Argentina, where it is linked to aylen, 'ember', or to words for 'clear' and 'laughing'. It is popular in Argentina.
From Portuguese and Galician lua, 'moon', from Latin luna, which makes it a sister form of Luna. Lua was also the name of a minor Roman goddess.

assoc.t: Lua, programming language used in Roblox and other games

e.note: In Hawaii lua is the everyday word for toilet or bathroom.

e.etymology: From an Irish surname, an Anglicized form of O Conghalaigh and O Conghaile, 'descendant of Conghalach'. It is the same family name as Connolly.
A modern American blend of Rae with the -leigh ending of Ryleigh and Kayleigh, which goes back to Old English leah, 'meadow, clearing'.
From an Old English name joining willa, 'will, desire', and maere, 'famous', which survived as a surname. Once a rural American favorite, it is now most used in Hispanic families.
namesakes: Wilmer Valderrama (actor, That '70s Show and NCIS)

e.etymology: A pet form of Linda, Lindsay, Melinda and Belinda. Its 1927 spike came from 'Lucky Lindy', the nickname of aviator Charles Lindbergh, which also named the Lindy Hop swing dance.

assoc.t: the Lindy Hop, swing dance of the 1920s and 30s
'Lucky Lindy', nickname of aviator Charles Lindbergh

e.etymology: The English word glory, from Latin gloria, used as a given name in the same spirit as the older and more common Gloria.

assoc.t: Glory, 1989 Civil War film with Denzel Washington

e.etymology: A modern American name that puts the -lynn ending on the Har- of Harper, Harlow and Harley. It also echoes the older surname name Harlan.
From the Spanish surname Cortez, a variant of Cortes, from cortes, 'courteous, polite'. As an American first name it peaked around 1990.
namesakes: Cortez Kennedy (Hall of Fame Seahawks defensive tackle)

assoc.t: Hernan Cortes, conquistador who toppled the Aztec Empire
Sea of Cortez, between Baja California and Mexico

e.note: Evokes the conquistador Hernan Cortes, whose conquest of the Aztecs is remembered as brutal.

e.etymology: A feminine form of Alan, a Breton name the Normans brought to Britain. Singer Alanis Morissette was named for her father, Alan. It is now most used in Hispanic families, where Alanis is also a surname.
namesakes: Alanis Morissette (singer-songwriter of Jagged Little Pill)

e.etymology: A spelling of Amira, the feminine of Arabic amir, 'prince, commander', from the verb amara, 'to command'.
A modern American coinage that puts the popular Ja- prefix on Nyla, in the pattern of Janiyah and Jaliyah.
A modern Indian name usually explained as 'full of life and energy'; its Sanskrit source is not well documented. It spread after Bollywood actress Shilpa Shetty chose it for her son in 2012.
A modern American name in the family of Aria, Araya and Amaya, spelled with the -yah ending of Aaliyah and Mariah. It has no established meaning of its own.
